item.title: JayQuery: Privacy-Preserving Student Success Prediction
item.description:
JayQuery was ADAL’s SCARP 2026 project on privacy-preserving student success prediction with federated learning.

Colleges are data-rich but insight-poor: FERPA regulations prevent offices such as the Registrar, Financial Aid and the learning management system from merging their student records into a single model. JayQuery uses vertical federated learning (VFL): separate data silos collaborate to train a dropout-risk predictor without ever sharing raw records. The silos align their records through a private set intersection (PSI) handshake, each trains a local “bottom” model, and a federated learning server combines their embeddings in a “top” model protected with differential-privacy noise.

Team

  • Alex Pellet, system architect and ML engineer
  • Wyatt Wilfong, privacy and security lead
  • Dr. Peilong Li, faculty mentor

item.title: NetSec: Accelerated Malware Detection with Machine Learning
item.description:
NetSec, Accelerated Malware Detection in Executable Files with Machine Learning, was supported by a SCARP 2022 grant and an Intel Academic Grant (2022), on which Dr. Li served as Co-PI.

Student teams built and evaluated machine-learning pipelines for malware detection, including:

  • a streaming inference pipeline using Apache Kafka on the IoT-23 network traffic dataset, and
  • an Intel-sponsored project (Fall 2022) comparing Random Forest, LightGBM and convolutional neural network models for classifying malicious and benign IoT network packets on the IoT-23 and TON_IoT datasets.

item.title: ANTA: Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning for Network Traffic Analysis
item.description:
ANTA (Accelerated Network Traffic Analytics) was ADAL’s SCARP 2020 project, A Performance Study between Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods on Network Traffic Analysis.

The team studied the problem of detecting TLS-encrypted malware using flow metadata and TLS features. They benchmarked a suite of widely used machine learning and deep learning models on two malware flow datasets, measuring classification accuracy as well as run-time performance (throughput, CPU and RAM utilization), and accelerated the detectors with Intel DAAL and OpenVINO.

Team

  • Matthew Grohotolski and Connor DiLeo, student researchers
  • Dr. Peilong Li, faculty mentor
  • Collaborators: Dr. Yan Luo and Onur Barut (University of Massachusetts Lowell) and Tong Zhang (Intel)

item.title: ACETA: Encrypted Network Traffic Analytics
item.description:
Introduction

Encrypted network traffic is the major form of the data transmitting over the Internet today. According to the statistics, 94% of all Google web traffic is encrypted as of July 2019. In 2019 alone, the encryption certificates issued per day is over 1 million. While protecting the privacy and providing security for enterprises, encryption technology also benefits evaders to secure their malicious activities.

Traditional solutions to identify network threats fall into two major categories: 1) deep packet inspection and signatures; and 2) offline network pattern modeling. However, the first category is not applicable on encrypted traffic. Furthermore, solutions that work on decrypted network data will compromise the user privacy and data integrity, and are computationally intensive. By passively monitoring malicious behaviors on a session-based level, the second category of traditional solutions demonstrate high accuracy and low false positives. However, training machine learning models, and inferencing with effective models in a timely fashion are challenging due to the high computational power and low response latency requirements.

With the recent adoption of network function virtualization (NFV) technology, enterprises start to deploy universal customer premises equipment (uCPE) on their network edge to perform complex network functionality including encrypted traffic analytics (ETA). Such uCPE equipments rely on commodity x86 platforms to enable virtual network functions provisioned without pre-configuration or manual operations. Meanwhile, recent innovation on x86 multicore systems, such as the Intel Data Analytics Acceleration Library (DAAL) for machine learning and the Intel OpenVINO toolkit for computer vision and neural networks, have enabled ETA to render faster training and inference and analyze larger data sets with available compute resources on x86 uCPE equipments. The library also exploits the next-generation processors such as Intel Xeon D to render optimal performance. By exploiting DAAL and OpenVINO, we can greatly accelerate the ETA speed without compromising performance.

In this project, we propose to leverage Intel x86 multicore platforms with the aforementioned software to design an ETA system named ACETA with accelerated model training and inference. Specifically, we contribute in the three following aspects. 1) We seek to study the Cisco’s open-sourced ETA software named Joy as the reference design, and extend Joy with three new machine learning models and test them with a new open-source dataset. 2) We optimize the ETA pipeline in the proposed software package ACETA with multithreading and Intel software packages to render faster training and inference speed without sacrificing performance. 3) We conduct thorough performance evaluation and comparison between Joy and ACETA for future reference.
